resume: Classify at least 8 situations out of 10 (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement) using the labels as justification, explain the role of the test set and give two examples in SHS.

diapos.notes: Prerequisite: the chapter 1 lesson “Supervised learning and unsupervised learning”. Prepare ten situation cards per group (the table in the lesson plan) and open the exercises of the chapter 1 tutorial (TD) on the site. Form groups of three or four, mixing levels and equipment.

points: **Classify** at least 8 situations out of 10: supervised, unsupervised or reinforcement
**Justify** each choice using the labels
**Explain** the role of the test set
**Give** two examples of learning in the humanities and social sciences
diapos.notes: The first objective has a numerical criterion: 8 situations out of 10. Announce it: it will give the groups a benchmark during the sorting.

consignes: In groups of three or four
Sort the ten cards into three piles: supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement
On each card, write down the decisive clue
Each group then defends one card in front of the class
diapos.notes: During the sorting, walk around and ask “what have you tried?” rather than giving the answer. Two cards are traps (Go and the spam filter): do not point them out. For the defense, draw the spokesperson at random: everyone must be ready. Only show the correction after the defenses.

diapos.titre: Correction: eight cards without a trap

colonnes.titre: Supervised: the examples carry the answer
points: Dating a poem using 600 dated poems
Estimating the year a poem was written (regression)
Classifying 3,000 speeches using 500 classified speeches
Detecting hateful comments using 5,000 annotated examples
Identifying the language of a message using labeled messages
Dividing 200 novels into stylistic families
Grouping 2,000 open-ended answers without a grid
Bringing out the themes of 1,000 articles

diapos.notes: For each card, have students state the clue: dated, classified, annotated or labeled examples → supervised; no grid, groups or themes to discover → unsupervised. The year of composition is a numerical label: this is regression, not classification. For the 3,000 speeches, recall the quiz in the lesson: it is normal that the new speeches have no label, because that is exactly what the model must predict.

diapos.question: “Learning Go by winning or losing games”: what type of learning is this?
diapos.explication: There are no corrected examples: the program plays, and winning or losing serves as its reward or penalty.
diapos.notes: Likely wrong answer: “unsupervised”, because there are no labels. Show the difference: here, the program learns by acting and receiving rewards. This is how AlphaGo Zero (DeepMind, 2017) learned Go by playing against itself. Reinforcement learning will be studied in chapter 3.

diapos.question: A filter learns from the emails that users have marked as “spam”. What type of learning is this?
diapos.explication: The user’s “spam” click is a label: each example carries the right answer.
diapos.notes: Likely wrong answers: “unsupervised”, because nobody annotated the emails on purpose, or “reinforcement”, because the filter improves with use. Yet each marked email carries the expected answer: that is exactly a label. Sorting emails into “spam” and “not spam” is the textbook example of supervised classification.

etapes.titre: Do the examples carry the answer?
etapes.texte: The question to ask for each situation, about the training examples
Classification if the answer is a category, regression if it is a number
The algorithm forms groups that the researcher must interpret
The program learns by acting and receiving rewards or penalties

diapos.notes: 10 min of sharing results. Write the question on the board: “Do the training examples carry the right answer?” It settles almost every case. Careful: look at the examples used for training, not at the new cases, which never have a label.

diapos.definition: The part of the data set aside to evaluate the model on examples it has never seen.
diapos.exemple: Like an exam made of questions the student has never seen.
diapos.notes: A rule to have students write down: a model is never evaluated on the examples used to train it. The data are split in two: the training set (jeu d’entraînement) fits the model; the test set, set aside, measures its performance at the end. The goal is generalization: handling new cases well.

diapos.definition: A flaw of a model that memorizes the details of the training set and generalizes poorly to new data.
diapos.exemple: Almost perfect in training, poor in the test: like the student who memorized the solutions without understanding the course.
diapos.notes: The warning sign: a large gap between the training score and the test score. In the lesson’s example, a model that is too complex learns the training poems by heart, with their accidental details, instead of grasping what characterizes each period.

diapos.question: All your Romantic poems come from old editions that write “enfans” for “enfants”. What does the model learn?
diapos.reponse: The spelling of the edition, rather than the style of the period.
diapos.explication: A model relies on anything that distinguishes the examples, even an accidental detail: a good score does not guarantee that it has learned what you are looking for.
diapos.notes: An example taken from the lesson. Let students think for a minute before showing the answer. A point to remember for literature students: knowing the origin of every text in the corpus (edition, spelling, digitization) is part of the method.

diapos.sousTitre: Exercises 1 to 3 in class, exercise 4 as homework
diapos.notes: The exercises are on the site, in the chapter 1 tutorial (TD). Ask students not to open “Show the solution” before the class correction.

consignes: Exercise 1: for supervised and unsupervised learning, a definition, the data, the tasks, one difficulty
Exercise 2: a comparison table of the two types of learning, written from memory
diapos.notes: Alone, then in pairs, then correction. The table in exercise 2 is written without notes: this is exactly what the exam asks for. If a pair finishes early, ask them where to place semi-supervised learning and self-supervised learning.

points: Data: examples with their **label** (an email and “spam”)
Tasks: classification, regression
Evaluation: comparing with the labels of the test set
Difficulty: annotating is costly; labels reflect the choices, sometimes the prejudices, of annotators
Data: examples **without labels**
Tasks: clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, topic modeling
Evaluation: coherence of the groups, usefulness for interpretation
Difficulty: naming and interpreting the groups obtained

diapos.notes: Add the in-between cases orally. Semi-supervised learning combines a few labeled examples with many raw examples. Self-supervised learning takes the label from the data itself, for example by hiding the next word of a sentence: this is how large language models are pre-trained. Reinforcement learning has no corrected examples: an agent receives rewards or penalties and learns the strategy that maximizes them.

lignes: Direct: labels of the test set
Indirect: coherence of the groups, human reading
Attributing an anonymous text to a known author
diapos.legende: In supervised learning, we learn to reproduce known answers; in unsupervised learning, we look for an organization that we do not know yet.
diapos.notes: Have students compare row by row with the pairs’ tables. Details of the “Algorithms” row: linear and logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, decision trees, neural networks; for unsupervised learning, principal component analysis (PCA) and LDA, for topic modeling. For evaluation: accuracy or mean error on one side, silhouette score on the other. Have students copy the summary sentence.

consignes: In pairs, find six examples of learning
For each one: the type of learning, the task, the data used
At least two examples from the humanities or from literature
diapos.notes: Above all, check that the type and the data are consistent: if labels are needed, the learning is supervised. Encourage examples taken from the course: poems, novels from the Maghreb, political speeches, messages in Darja, surveys on reading.

lignes: Attributing a disputed text to an author (stylometry)
Estimating when a poem was written
Respondent profiles in a survey on reading
Learning Go by playing against oneself
Games; winning serves as the reward
diapos.legende: Other answers are possible: check that the type is consistent with the data.
diapos.notes: The SHS examples: stylometry, which Mosteller and Wallace applied in 1964 to some of the *Federalist Papers*; the date of a poem; reader profiles. Go refers to AlphaGo Zero (DeepMind, 2017). Have each pair read out one example: the class says whether the type and the data match.

consignes: Can today’s computers do these six tasks? One task per pair
Play ping-pong properly · drive a car in a city center · discover and prove theorems
Write a funny story · give a relevant legal opinion · perform a complex surgical operation
Define the success criterion: compared with whom, under what conditions?
A 3-minute report at the next session
diapos.notes: Share out the six tasks, even if it means giving the same task to several pairs. Stress the words in the instructions: “properly”, “relevant”, “funny”; defining these criteria is part of the work. Do not show the solution on the site: it is a state of knowledge from September 2026, in a field that changes very fast. Students will have to check what has changed since then.

etapes.texte: Compared with a beginner, a professional, the best human? Under what conditions?
Peer-reviewed articles, technical reports; preprints (arXiv, HAL) with caution
A company presenting its own product is not a neutral source
Number of trials, environment, opponents, share of human supervision, failure rate
Date of the result, date you consulted it; at least two independent sources

diapos.notes: This method applies to any documentary research on AI. Preprints are useful but have not always been peer-reviewed; Google Scholar helps you find articles. To cross-check, a general overview such as the book by Jean-Gabriel Ganascia (*L’IA expliquée aux humains*, 2024), cited in the course references, can serve as a second source. Nuances are the expected answer, not an admission of weakness.

points: “Unsupervised” does not mean “without humans”: the researcher chooses, then interprets
The new cases have no label: that is no reason to conclude it is unsupervised
**Classification**: known categories; **clustering**: discovered groups
diapos.notes: For each mistake, have students find the card that shows it. First mistake: the researcher chooses the data and the number of groups, then interprets; the 200 novels do not sort themselves into “families”. Second: the 3,000 speeches. Third: dating a poem using 600 dated poems (classification) versus dividing 200 novels into stylistic families (clustering).

sous: The site’s solution dates from September 2026: check what has changed since then

points: **Reread** “AI approaches to problem solving” (chapter 1)
**Learn** the glossary, in French and in English
diapos.texte: Next session: first Python lab session (TP)
diapos.notes: Before ending the class, check the numerical objective with a show of hands: who classified at least 8 cards out of 10? The glossary is learned in pairs: one French → English card and one English → French card, with the definition on the back.
